body: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present , a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], p = 5.82 × 10-8) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0% vs.\ 15.4%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta () convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0% vs.\ 62.5% for Fixed-3) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4×. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9% for a Self-Refine critic, p = 0.61) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.
